File image/Reuters FP Tech Desk | Nov 11, 2026, 11:26:40 IST Microsoft's growing investment in artificial intelligence is drawing criticism from within the company, with employees questioning how its push towards AI is affecting working conditions, job security and its wider responsibilities.

The concerns have emerged as the tech giant offers voluntary exits to approximately 60,000 employees , the largest buyout programme in its history. The development has added to questions about employee morale at a time when Microsoft is committing increasingly large sums to AI infrastructure and data centres.

An open letter signed by a group calling itself 'Concerned Microsoft Workers' outlines several objections to the company's direction. According to The New York Times, the letter began circulating among employees before Microsoft announced its latest buyout programme on October 26.
The signatories include current and former employees, as well as workers associated with subsidiaries such as LinkedIn and GitHub. Vendors, interns and contractors are also welcome to join the group.

The letter raises concerns about how Microsoft's AI strategy is being implemented internally. Employees say they are increasingly expected to incorporate AI tools into their daily responsibilities, even when the benefits are unclear and adequate training has not been provided.

According to the signatories, adopting these tools can create additional work. Employees must learn new systems, check their output for errors and sometimes undo changes or features that do not work as intended. They argue that the emphasis on speed overlooks the time and effort required to make AI-generated results usable.

The group is also concerned about the growing connection between AI adoption and employee performance. It wants Microsoft to stop using AI usage as a basis for workplace rewards or negative assessments, arguing that staff should have a say in deciding how these technologies are introduced.

Beyond internal working conditions, the letter questions Microsoft's approach to AI safety and its commercial relationships. Signatories cite concerns about user protection in the company's research into AI agents and allege that internal planning documents discuss ways of encouraging people to become increasingly dependent on AI products.

The group has also objected to Microsoft's contracts with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Israeli military. It has questioned the financial relationships between major AI companies, describing their investments as a cycle of money flowing between a relatively small group of businesses.

Environmental commitments form another part of the demands. Employees want Microsoft to maintain its 2030 goals of becoming carbon negative, water positive and achieving zero waste. They have also called for greater transparency around data centre projects and stronger safeguards for communities affected by their development.
The letter's broader message is that decisions about AI should involve workers and local communities, rather than being driven solely by the company's business priorities.

The criticism comes as Microsoft undertakes another significant workforce exercise. Its latest Voluntary Exit Offer is available to eligible employees at level 70 and below in selected teams across India, the US, the UK and Canada. Certain sales and engineering teams are not included.

Employees accepting the offer will receive at least eight weeks of base salary, with the final payout depending on their level and tenure. They have until December 9 to accept, with departures scheduled for December 31.

Chief people officer Amy Coleman described the programme in an internal communication as an opportunity for employees to make a career transition with financial assistance. Microsoft expects fewer than 5 per cent of eligible workers to take up the offer.
Coleman has said the buyouts are not connected to the changes AI is bringing to people's jobs. However, she has not ruled out additional workforce reductions.

The latest offer follows other restructuring exercises during 2026. In April, Microsoft offered early retirement to approximately 8,600 long-serving employees in the US, around 30 per cent of whom accepted. In July, it eliminated roughly 4,800 positions, including about a fifth of its Xbox workforce . These decisions followed around 10,000 job cuts in 2023 and more than 15,000 in 2025. Microsoft's workforce stood at 223,000 in June, down 5,000 from the previous year.
Employees have also questioned the difference between the company's financial performance and the rewards reaching its workforce.
issues.digest: 微软正因AI战略面临内部反弹。一群自称“关切微软员工”的现任与前任员工发布公开信，质疑公司AI优先方针，指出员工被要求使用AI工具却缺乏培训，且AI使用情况被纳入绩效评估，增加工作负担。信中还对AI安全、与ICE及以色列军方的合同、环境承诺等提出异议。与此同时，微软推出史上最大规模自愿离职计划，覆盖四国约6万人，引发对裁员与AI替代岗位的担忧。员工质疑公司财务表现与员工回报脱节，呼吁决策应吸纳员工和社区意见。
points: 员工批评AI工具强制采用，缺乏培训且增加纠错负担，AI使用不应作为奖惩依据
公开信质疑微软与ICE及以色列军方合同，并担忧AI依赖和商业循环投资问题
微软推出覆盖约6万人的自愿离职计划，员工质疑AI与裁员关联，要求保障环境承诺
